blocks.text: In 1970, while I was touring Western countries, I had the opportunity to visit several parts of the city of London. There is a beautiful place called “Hyde Park” (HydePark)! One could even call it a public-speaking arena. Here and there across that park, in broad open spaces and on green lawns, hundreds of people stand in circles. And not merely in one place like this—in many places!

segments.text: At each of those places, someone will be standing on a table, or on a stool, or on some kind of platform, speaking in a loud voice. A crowd gathers around him just as crowds gather around a street performer in our towns. Those speakers use that place itself as their training ground and speak. There is no restriction on what they may say there. They will even attack the British royal line to their heart’s content. They will severely analyse problems concerning various countries.

segments.text: அவை நடுக்கம்—அதாவது சபைக் கூச்சம்—அதிலிருந்து ஒருவன் மீண்டுவிட்டால், அவன் நல்ல பேச்சாளனாக வாய்ப்புப் பெற்று விட்டான் என்று கூறிவிடலாம். இன்றைக்கு மேடை அதிர முழங்குகிற பல பேச்சாளர்கள் தங்களது முதல் மேடைப் பேச்சின்போது உடலிலுள்ள நாடி நரம்புகள் எல்லாம் அதிக வியர்வை வழிந்தோட—நாக் குழற மேடையில் நின்றிருப்பார்கள் என்பதை மறந்து விடாதீர்கள்.

“இதுடன் என் பேச்சை முடித்துக்கொள்கிறேன்”
என்று கூறுவதற்குப் பதிலாக—

segments.text: ஒரு பெரும் பட அதிபர், நாடகம் காண வந்திருந்தார். திடீரென சிவாஜி அவர்கள் அவரை மேடைக்கு அழைத்து மாலை அணிவித்து இரண்டு வார்த்தை வாழ்த்துமாறு கேட்டுக் கொண்டார். அந்தப் பட அதிபர் ஒலிபெருக்கியின் முன்னால் நின்றார். கை கால்கள் உதறல் எடுத்தன. எத்தனையோ இயக்குநர்களை, நடிகர், நடிகைகளை, திரையுலக நிபுணர்களை உருவாக்கிய பெரியவர் அவர்! நூற்றுக்கணக்கானவர்கள் அவரது நிறுவனத்தில் பணிபுரிகிற அளவுக்கு படத்துறையில் சிறந்த அனுபவம் பெற்றவர். இந்தி மொழியிலும் கூடப் படங்கள் எடுத்து, தமிழகத்துக் கலைத் திறனை வெளிப்படுத்தியவர். மலை போன்ற உருவம் கொண்டவர். அப்படிப்பட்டவர் ஒலிபெருக்கியின் முன்னால் நின்றவுடன் வியர்வைக் கடலில் மிதந்தார். இறுதியாக அவர் பேசியது என்ன தெரியுமா?

blocks.text: I was fifteen then! Gathering together some student friends who studied with me and some young friends from the street where I lived, I started an organisation called the “Children’s Reform Association” in a thatched hut. Only those who paid a quarter-anna would be admitted as members. Every week they had to pay one paisa as a subscription for the Association’s development work.

blocks.text: As mentioned in the first part of my autobiographical notes, “Nenjukku Neethi,” the Association that had been in the thatched hut was soon shifted—to a dilapidated Anjaneya temple. Even before that, I would seat seven or eight boys in that thatched hut and, as the leader of the Association, speak to them.

segments.text: The boys should conduct themselves with cleanliness and discipline. They should not fall prey to bad habits such as beedis and cigarettes. No one should speak words that could cause harm. I would give them advice of this kind.

segments.text: The house next to that thatched hut was the home of the late Isaimani T. V. Namasivayam! Namasivayam was a friend from my youth. It was his uncles—T. N. Raman and T. N. Lachappa—who then shone in that area as flames of the Self-Respect Movement. T. N. Raman was also one who stood in the forefront with T. M. Parthasarathy, Jalakandapuram Kannan and others in the effort to hold the function at which song-poet Bharathidasan was presented with a purse by Arignar Anna, and who brought out a Bharathidasan souvenir!

segments.text: I often happened to meet people with such political and social involvement at my friend Namasivayam’s home. Because of that, I was able to see many books and periodicals. I was able to read and understand the views of many political leaders.

segments.text: Only if it is in the pot can it come into the ladle. This is a proverb that still echoes in our villages. In the same way, if one is to speak—even before a gathering of ten—doesn’t one first have to know something? The habit of reading books written by many leaders—newspapers—weekly and monthly magazines, eagerly waiting to buy and read them—these had filled the pot that was my mind. I had understood the political and social problems that could be understood at that age. That was why I was able to speak without trembling at those thatched-hut meetings. That preparation was of great help in the stage-speaking competition held at the high school I attended.

I had understood the political and social problems that could be understood at that age. That was why I was able to speak without trembling at those thatched-hut meetings. That preparation was of great help in the stage-speaking competition held at the high school I attended.

segments.text: Once a person gets over stage fright—that is, shyness before an assembly—you may say he has gained the chance to become a good speaker. Do not forget: many speakers who today roar until the stage shakes would have stood during their first stage speech with every vein and nerve in their bodies running with sweat—their tongues faltering.

segments.text: சங்க இலக்கிய நூல் ஒன்றுக்கு உரையெழுதக்கூடிய அளவுக்குச் சொற்களைப் புரிந்து வைத்துக் கொள்ள வேண்டிய அவசியம் பேச்சாளருக்குத் தேவையில்லை. அதற்காக அத்தனை சொற்களையும் தெரிந்து வைத்துக் கொள்ள வேண்டுமென்று நான் கூறவும் மாட்டேன். அவற்றையும் தெரிந்து வைத்துக்கொண்டால் அவர்கள் மேலும் ஆற்றல் மிக்க பேச்சாளர்களாக ஒளிவிடமுடியும். அது மட்டுமின்றி, வளர்ந்துவரும் அறிவுலகத்தில் நாள் தோறும் புதிய புதிய சொற்கள் பிறந்துகொண்டேயிருக்கின்றன. அவற்றையெல்லாம் அறிந்து வைத்துக்கொள்ள வேண்டியது ஒரு பேச்சாளரின் கடமையாகும்.

segments.text: “அடியேன் பேசப்போகும் விஷயத்தில் குற்றம் குறைகள் இருக்கலாம். அப்படி இருக்குமேயானால் சபையோர்களாகிய நீங்கள், எப்படி பாலையும் தண்ணீரையும் கலந்து வைத்தால் அன்னப்பட்சியானது பாலை மட்டும் பருகிவிட்டு, தண்ணீரை விட்டு விடுகிறதோ அதைப்போல எனது பேச்சில் உள்ள நிறைகளை மட்டும் எடுத்துக் கொண்டு குறைகளை விட்டுவிடுமாறு கேட்டுக் கொள்கிறேன்.

segments.text: “அவையோர்களே!சர்க்கரையையும் மணலையும் கலந்து வைத்தால்,எப்படி எறும்பானது மணலை விடுத்துச் சர்க்கரையை மட்டும் தின்றிடுமோ அதைப் போலும்—இரும்புத்தூளையும் மரத்தூளையும் கலந்து வைத்தால்,எப்படிக் காந்தமானது இரும்புத்தூளை மட்டும் இழுத்துக்கொள்ளுமோ அதைப் போலும்—என் பேச்சில் குறைகளைத் தள்ளிவிட்டு, நிறைகளை ஏற்றிடுமாறு கேட்டுக்கொள்கிறேன்.”

segments.text: Our forebears divided Tamil into three: iyal—music—koothu. Countless years ago, in that age when human beings roamed naked and later tied leaves and foliage around themselves, covering only the organs below the waist, it could not possibly have been that iyal came first, music second, and koothu third! Iyal is based on words; music is based on sound! Koothu is based on movement!

segments.text: In the beginning, human beings had no knowledge of language at all. When a person saw a stone or a tree, a mountain or a river, he gave none of them any name. So there was no need for words to arise. It was only through gestures that people began to make things understood to one another. Waving their hands, nodding their heads, they lived like mute people.

blocks.text: After that, they made one kind of sound to call someone far away and another kind of sound to make someone nearby turn toward them. Through sound-signals such as “ஏ” “ஓ” “ஈ”, they communicated with one another. Only as a third stage did human society begin using words suited to the respective regions in which it lived!

segments.text: Even though iyal now stands first among iyal, music and koothu, in the earliest period, after humankind had appeared but before it had grown and undergone many changes, people lived through movements—gestures, and so koothu occupied first place then. Music, based on sound, was then—and is now—in the middle. Iyal, which had been third, came and sat in first place because it operates on words—and those words became necessary for music and likewise necessary for koothu.

segments.text: Only by choosing and using those words can one skilfully handle both the art of writing and the art of speaking.

blocks.text: Only by choosing and using those words can one skilfully handle both the art of writing and the art of speaking.

segments.text: Choosing words does not mean keeping a dictionary, memorising words, and trying to work out how to fit them into our speech!

blocks.text: Choosing words does not mean keeping a dictionary, memorising words, and trying to work out how to fit them into our speech!

segments.text: By reading many books, newspapers, weeklies and monthlies, new words become familiar to us. When we speak, they should come of their own accord and fall into place. We should not climb onto a stage and stand there searching for suitable words sentence by sentence. To some extent, we ourselves must be a dictionary. Even if we cannot be a great dictionary, we must know many words.

segments.text: A speaker does not need to understand enough words to write a commentary on a work of Sangam literature. I will not say that a speaker must know all those words for that. If speakers know them too, they can shine as still more powerful speakers. Not only that: in the expanding world of knowledge, new words are being born every day. It is the duty of a speaker to know them all.

segments.text: In earlier days, however great the speakers or leaders, once they mounted the stage they would spend a few minutes on a preamble before speaking.

segments.text: “There may be faults and shortcomings in what this humble one is about to say. If so, I ask you, members of the audience: just as the swan, when milk and water are mixed, drinks only the milk and leaves the water, take only the merits in my speech and leave the shortcomings.

segments.text: Speeches in the old days used to be like this. When I first began speaking on stage, I too used this same preamble with another comparison.

segments.text: “Members of the audience! Just as, if sugar and sand are mixed, the ant leaves the sand and eats only the sugar—and just as, if iron filings and wood dust are mixed, the magnet draws only the iron filings—I ask you likewise to cast aside the faults in my speech and accept its merits.”

segments.text: Back then, I thought I had done something novel simply by replacing the swan and milk in this way!

the audience will certainly feel affection and fondness for that young person.

segments.text: Many young people mount the stage after memorising a speech. If even a small interruption occurs while they recite what they have learned in a fluster, they stand bewildered and try to begin their memorised speech all over again from the start! Do not load their brains with weighty matters—place in them only the matters they know from current affairs. Only then will they themselves understand what they are speaking about.

segments.text: “Like Socrates, the wise elder of Athens—like Karl Marx, who sowed the seed of thought for the garden of communism—like Ingersoll, who found light in darkness—the lion of self-respect, Thanthai Periyar, shone.”

segments.text: For a young speaker who memorises what has been written out like this and speaks on a stage, should he not know who Socrates is? Should that young speaker not understand Marx and Ingersoll as well?

segments.text: Therefore, a young speaker speaking at a Periyar function should be taught only what can be made to stick in his mind.

segments.text: “Periyar laboured to abolish castes! Periyar rejected the claim that human beings were born as one caste from Brahma’s face, one caste from his shoulder, one caste from his thigh, and one caste from his feet, and thundered that all are one clan—the human clan.”

segments.text: Only when a young speaker is trained in this simple way, in a simple style, can the words his lips utter be connected to his heart. Only when that connection exists can he express those ideas with feeling.

segments.text: A victorious Legislative Assembly member once took me to a felicitation function in his constituency. Speaking at the first event, he said:
“People of the constituency! During the election I had given you a big promise. Namely, that if you made me win, I would bring Kalaignar! Now I have brought him and fulfilled the promise!”

During the election I had given you a big promise. Namely, that if you made me win, I would bring Kalaignar! Now I have brought him and fulfilled the promise!”

segments.text: Next, when I spoke, I said,
“The promise that I would be brought here is not such a big one! It is only a cheap promise! I am always meeting the people.”

blocks.text: Next, when I spoke, I said, “The promise that I would be brought here is not such a big one! It is only a cheap promise! I am always meeting the people.”

segments.text: Later, another meeting at another place in the same constituency! The Legislative Assembly member welcomed me and spoke there too. Do you know what he said?

blocks.text: Later, another meeting at another place in the same constituency! The Legislative Assembly member welcomed me and spoke there too. Do you know what he said?

segments.text: “People of the constituency! During the election I had given you a cheap promise. That was the promise that, if you made me win, I would bring Kalaignar!”

segments.text: Those near me were startled as soon as he said that. I kept smiling. That was what came of the member thinking that he too should use the very word I had used with a sense of humility at the first meeting in that constituency!

segments.text: He did not even understand the meaning of the word ‘cheap’! What was in the mind was one thing! What came out on the lips was another!

segments.text: From this, is it not clear that two things are essential for speakers—knowing many words, and keeping a connection between the heart and the words they utter?

segments.text: நெஞ்சம், சொற் பஞ்சமுடையதாயிருந்தால் மேடைப் பேச்சால் மக்களைக் கவர்ந்திட இயலாது. சிலருக்கு மனத்தில் நல்ல கருத்துக்கள் தோன்றும். அவற்றை வெளிப்படுத்த உரிய சொற்கள் இல்லாமல் தவித்திடுவர். வேறு சிலருக்குச் சிறந்த கருத்துக்களும் அவற்றை வெளிப்படுத்தக் கூடிய சொற்களும்கூட உள்ளத்தில் நிறைந்திருக்கும். ஆனால் அப்படிக் கிடைத்த வாய்ப்பைப் பயன்படுத்தக்கூடிய பேச்சுவன்மை அவர்களுக்கு வாய்க்காமல் போய்விடக் கூடும்.

segments.text: இளம் பேச்சாளனாக இருந்த நான் ஒரு முறை குடந்தையில் ஒரு கூட்டத்தில் பேசினேன். குடந்தைப் பெரியவர் கே. கே. நீலமேகம் தலைமையில் அந்தக் கூட்டம் நடந்ததாக நினைவு. அறிஞர் அண்ணா அவர்கள் சொற்பொழிவாற்ற வந்திருந்தார். என்னையும் பேசுமாறு கூறினார்கள். மிகக் குறைந்த நேரமே பேசி மக்களின் கைத்தட்டலையும் உற்சாக ஆரவாரத்தையும் பெற்றேன்.

segments.text: “காங்கிரஸ் கட்சியைச் சேர்ந்த சின்ன அண்ணாமலை ஒரு கூட்டத்தில் பேசினாராம்! அவர் மலையாம்! அண்ணா அவர்கள் துரையாம்! மலையில் மழை பெய்தால்தான் துரைக்கு வருமாம்! அதனால் அண்ணாதுரையை விட அண்ணாமலையே மேல்! இப்படிப் பேசிய அண்ணாமலை அவர்களுக்குச் சொல்லிக் கொள்வேன் அந்த மலையில் பொழியவேண்டிய மழைக்குத் தேவையான மேகம், இதோ எங்களிடம் இருக்கிறது! அதுதான் கே. கே. நீலமேகம்!”

segments.text: நல்ல உடற்கட்டும், நிமிர்ந்த நோக்கும், கொள்கை உறுதியும் கொண்ட பெரியவர் நீலமேகம், தமது வரவேற்புரையை எழுதியே படித்தார். எழுதிப் படிக்கும் நீண்ட உரைகளை மக்கள் ஆர்வத்துடன் கேட்பதில்லை. அதிலும் அன்று அவரது உரை மிக மிக நீண்ட உரை! அத்துடன் பிற்பகல் உணவு வேளையும் நெருங்கிவிட்டது. அடுக்கி வைத்திருந்த தாள்களில் 25-ம் பக்கத்திற்குப் பிறகு 26-ஆம் பக்கம் விட்டுப்போய் 27-ஆம் பக்கத்தைப் படித்தார். பேச்சின் தொடர்பு அறுந்துபோயிற்று, மாநாட்டுப் பந்தலில் கேலிச் சிரிப்பும் கைத்தட்டலும் எழுந்தது. கே. கே. என். அவர்களுக்குக் கடுங்கோபம் வந்து விட்டது!

segments.text: இப்படி அவர் கர்ச்சனை செய்தபிறகு பந்தலில் அமைதி ஏற்பட்டது. எழுதிப் படிக்கிற உரைகளானாலும் அவற்றை ஒரு முறைக்கு இருமுறை கவனமாகப் படித்து, பக்க எண்களைச் சரியாகக் குறித்து ஒழுங்காக அடுக்கி வைத்துக்கொண்டு மக்களைக் கவரும் வகையில் குரலை உயர்த்திப் பேசவேண்டும் என்பதற்கு எடுத்துக் காட்டாகவே இந்த நிகழ்ச்சியை நினைவுபடுத்தினேன்.

segments.text: நாடக உலகிலும் திரையுலகிலும் ஓரளவு புகழ்பெற்ற நடிகர் ஒருவர் என்னுடன் பல ஆண்டுகளுக்கு முன்பு ஒரு பொதுக்கூட்டத்தில் பேச ஆரணிக்கு வந்திருந்தார். அவர் பேச்சாளர் என்று அறிவித்ததும் நல்ல வரவேற்பு இருந்தது. தொடக்கத்தில் கடல்மடை திறந்தாற்போல் வார்த்தைகளைக் கொட்டினார். அவருடைய நினைவு எங்கேயோ இருந்திருக்கிறது! மக்கள் முன் எடுத்து வைத்த கருத்துக்களோடு அவர் ஒன்றியிருக்கவில்லை. பேசிக்கொண்டே இருந்தவர், திடீரெனத் திகைத்து நின்றுவிட்டார். ஒரு நிமிடத்திற்கு மேல் அப்படியே நின்றார். பேசிக்கொண்டு வந்த பொருள் பற்றிய தொடர்பை அப்படியே விட்டுவிட்டு அவர்
“இத்துடன் என் பேச்சை முடித்துக் கொள்கிறேன்”
எனக் கூறி அமர்ந்துவிட்டார்.

segments.text: இதிலிருந்து புரிவதென்ன? ஒரு பேச்சாளன் மக்களுக்குச் சொல்ல முயன்ற கருத்துக்களுடன் தானும் உண்மையிலேயே இரண்டறக் கலந்திருந்தால்தான் தங்கு தடையின்றிப் பேசமுடியும்! எங்கேயோ மனத்தை உலவவிட்டு விட்டு, அரங்கின் முன்னே உதடுகளை அசைத்துக் கொண்டிருந்தால் உணர்வு பூர்வமான பேச்சாக அமையாது!

segments.text: சொற்பொழிவைக் கேட்பதற்கு மக்கள் சங்கீதம் கேட்க வருவது போல் வந்த காலத்தை உருவாக்கிய பெருமை அண்ணா அவர்களுக்கு உண்டு!

blocks.text: சொற்பொழிவைக் கேட்பதற்கு மக்கள் சங்கீதம் கேட்க வருவது போல் வந்த காலத்தை உருவாக்கிய பெருமை அண்ணா அவர்களுக்கு உண்டு!

segments.text: முப்பது ஆண்டுகளுக்கு மேலாகிறது; சென்னை சேத்துப்பட்டுப் பகுதியில் அண்ணா பேசுகிறார் என்று விளம்பரம் செய்யப்பட்டிருந்தது. நான், கவிஞர் கண்ணதாசன், அரங்கண்ணல், முல்லை சக்தி ஆகியோர் ஒரு காரில் அந்த இடம் நோக்கிப் புறப்பட்டோம். இரவு எட்டு மணியிருக்கும். கூட்டம் நடைபெறும் இடம் சரியாகத் தெரியவில்லை. ஒரு வெற்றிலை பாக்குக் கடையோரமாகக் காரை நிறுத்திவிட்டு
“அய்யா! இங்கே கூட்டம் எங்கே நடக்கிறது?”
என்று விசாரித்தோம்! கடை வாசலில் வாழைப்பழம் உரித்துத் தின்று கொண்டிருந்த ஒருவர் எங்களைப் பார்த்து,
“அதுவா! அண்ணாத்துரை கச்சேரி தானே? இப்படி இடது பக்கமாகத் திரும்பிப் போங்க!”
என்று பதில் அளித்து வழி காட்டினார்.

segments.text: சொற்பொழிவை ஒரு இசைக் கச்சேரியாகவே கருதிக் கொண்டனர். 1953-ல் நான் கல்லக்குடி போராட்டத்தில் ஈடுபட்டு திருச்சி சிறையில் இருந்தபோது, அங்கிருந்த ஒரு சாதாரணக் கைதி என்னைப் பார்த்து கைக்கூப்பி,
“நமஸ்காரங்க!”
என்று சொன்னார்.
“என்னைத் தெரியுமா?”
என்று அவரைக் கேட்டேன்.
“ஓ! நல்லாத் தெரியுமே! மூணு மாசத்துக்கு முன்பு மணப்பாறையிலே கச்சேரிக்கு வந்திருந்தீங்களே”

என்றார் அந்தக் கைதி! கூட்டங்களையே கச்சேரி என்று நினைத்துக் கொண்டிருந்த அந்த நிலையை கடந்த எவ்வளவு தூரம் தமிழ்நாடு முன்னேறியிருக்கிறது என்பதை எண்ணிப் பார்க்கவே மகிழ்ச்சியாக இருக்கிறதல்லவா? இவ்விதம் முன்னேறியுள்ள பேசும் கலையில் வல்லவர்களாகத் திகழ, பெரும் உழைப்பைத் தர வேண்டும் என்பதைப் பேச்சாளர்களாக விரும்புவோர் புரிந்துகொள்ள வேண்டும்.

segments.text: “அக்ராசனாதிபதி அவர்களே!”
என்று விளித்தது மாறி—
“அவைத்தலைவர் அவர்களே!”
என்று தமிழில் ஒலிக்கிற காலம் இது!
“ஸ்ரீமான் அவர்கள்!”
என்பது
“திருவாளர் அவர்கள்”

என்று மாறியிருக்கிற காலம் இது! இந்த மாற்றங்கள் ஏற்படுவதற்கு எழுத்தாளர்கள் மட்டும்மல்ல; தமிழ்ப்பற்று கொண்ட சொற்பொழிவாளர்களும் காரணமல்லவா? கூட்டங்களில் பேசிப்பேசி அந்தச் சொற்களை மக்களின் உள்ளத்தில் பதிய வைத்துவிட்டதால் அல்லவா; அவை பழகிப் போய்விட்டன! தமிழ் நூல்களை நிறையப் படிப்பதன் மூலமும், நல்ல தமிழ் ஏடுகளைத் தவறாமல் படிப்பதன் மூலமும் ஒரு தமிழ்ப் பேச்சாளர், தங்கு தடையற்ற தமிழ்ச் சொற்களைப் பயன்படுத்தும் ஆற்றலைப் பெற முடியும்.

segments.text: If the heart suffers from a famine of words, stage speech cannot captivate the people. Good ideas arise in the minds of some, but they struggle without the right words to express them. Others may have both excellent ideas and the words to express them filling their minds. Yet they may still lack the power of speech needed to make use of such an opportunity.

segments.text: Many senior scholars who have researched several languages and earned degrees have failed because they could not deliver a lecture in a way that drew in the audience seated before them. A speaker may deliberately practise at first how to raise and lower the voice to suit a speech, and what kinds of words to use; as time goes on, these habits will come naturally.

segments.text: The moment one learns to speak beautifully for five minutes, one must not nurture a desire to speak at a conference where fifty thousand people have gathered. At such conferences, one should closely observe what the leaders and the front-ranking members of those parties say, and how they attract the people.

segments.text: When I was a young speaker, I once spoke at a meeting in Kudanthai. As I remember, the meeting was chaired by the elder K. K. Neelamegam of Kudanthai. Arignar Anna had come to deliver an address. I too was asked to speak. I spoke for only a very short time and won the applause and enthusiastic cheers of the people.

Arignar Anna had come to deliver an address. I too was asked to speak. I spoke for only a very short time and won the applause and enthusiastic cheers of the people.

segments.text: “They say Chinna Annamalai of the Congress Party spoke at a meeting! He, they say, is a malai—a mountain! Anna, they say, is a durai—a lord! Only if rain falls on the malai will it come to the durai, they say! So Annamalai is above Annadurai! To Annamalai, who spoke like this, I would say: here with us is the megam—the cloud—needed for the rain that must fall on that malai! That is K. K. Neelamegam!”

segments.text: At meetings, people sometimes clap in appreciation! Sometimes they clap to tell the speaker to finish! I want to point here to an occasion when the K. K. Neelamegam I just mentioned delivered the welcome address at a conference held in Kudanthai.

segments.text: The elder Neelamegam, with a fine physique, an upright gaze and firmness of principle, had written out his welcome address and read it. People do not listen with interest to long speeches that are read from writing. And that day his speech was very, very long! The afternoon meal hour was approaching too. In his stack of pages, after page 25 he skipped page 26 and read page 27. The thread of the speech broke; mocking laughter and applause rose in the conference pavilion. K. K. N. became furious!

segments.text: “Whether anyone listens or not! As long as even one person remains in this pavilion, I will read my speech to the finish.”

blocks.text: “Whether anyone listens or not! As long as even one person remains in this pavilion, I will read my speech to the finish.”

segments.text: After he roared like this, silence settled over the pavilion. I recalled this incident only as an example to show that even speeches read from writing must be read carefully once or twice beforehand, their page numbers marked correctly and the sheets arranged in order, and then delivered with the voice raised in a way that attracts the people.

segments.text: Many years ago, an actor who had gained some fame in the world of drama and cinema came with me to Arani to speak at a public meeting. There was a good reception when he was announced as a speaker. At the beginning he poured out words as though a sea-sluice had been opened. His mind must have been somewhere else! He had not become one with the ideas he was placing before the people. As he went on speaking, he suddenly stopped, bewildered. He stood like that for more than a minute. Abandoning the thread of the subject he had been speaking about, he said,
“With this I conclude my speech,”
and sat down.

segments.text: What do we understand from this? Only if a speaker has truly merged inseparably with the ideas he is trying to tell the people can he speak without stumbling or obstruction! If he lets his mind wander somewhere else while merely moving his lips before the gathering, it will not become speech filled with feeling!

segments.text: Anna deserves the credit for creating an age when people came to hear a speech as though they were coming to listen to music!

segments.text: More than thirty years have passed; it had been announced that Anna would speak in the Chetpet area of Chennai. I, poet Kannadasan, Arangannal and Mullai Sakthi set out in a car toward the place. It must have been around eight at night. We did not know exactly where the meeting was being held. We stopped the car by a betel-and-areca-nut shop and asked,
“Ayya! Where is the meeting being held here?”
A man standing at the shop entrance peeling and eating a banana looked at us and replied,
“That one? The Annathurai kachcheri, isn't it? Turn this way to the left and go!”
He showed us the way.

segments.text: They thought of a speech itself as a musical kachcheri. In 1953, when I was in Trichy prison after taking part in the Kallakudi agitation, an ordinary prisoner there looked at me, folded his hands and said,
“Namaskaaranga!”
I asked him,
“Do you know me?”
“Oh! I know you very well! Three months ago you came to Manapparai for a kachcheri, didn't you?”

said that prisoner! Is it not a joy even to think how far Tamil Nadu has advanced from that stage when meetings themselves were thought of as kachcheris? Those who wish to become speakers must understand that, to excel in this art of speaking that has advanced so far, they must labour hard.

segments.text: This is an age in which the address
“Agraasanadhipathi avargale!”
has changed and the Tamil words
“Avai-thalaivar avargale!”
ring out! This is an age in which
“Sriman avargal!”
has changed into
“Thiruvalar avargal!”

Were writers alone responsible for these changes? Were not speakers with love for Tamil responsible too? Is it not because they spoke and spoke at meetings, planting those words in the hearts of the people, that the words became familiar! By reading many Tamil books, and by unfailingly reading good Tamil journals, a Tamil speaker can gain the ability to use Tamil words without stumbling or obstruction.

segments.text: If speakers merely graze the tips of the grass, at every meeting they will keep grinding the same flour that has already been ground. They do not even pick up and look at the new items of news appearing each day in the journals.

segments.text: Some speakers prepare one speech and go around for a whole year with it. After that, they prepare another speech and set out again. There is nothing wrong in stating at another place an idea used in one place, or in using a comparison used elsewhere! But only if there are changes in the angle from which they are presented will the speech gain lustre! If the same words—the same sentence structure—are used again and again like a recorded tape, those hearing that speaker for the second or third time will grow tired.

segments.text: Kalaivaanar N. S. Krishnan would conduct a wedding in Chennai every year for one of the boys or girls in his family. The wedding celebration would be held on a grand scale. Periyar, Anna and Jeeva would unfailingly attend those weddings. Some poets would attend too.

blocks.text: Kalaivaanar N. S. Krishnan would conduct a wedding in Chennai every year for one of the boys or girls in his family. The wedding celebration would be held on a grand scale. Periyar, Anna and Jeeva would unfailingly attend those weddings. Some poets would attend too.

segments.text: One poet—I do not wish to mention his name—would invariably be among those who blessed the couple. Though he called himself a man of progressive ideas, in the name of humour he would mock educated women merely to make the wedding guests laugh.

blocks.text: One poet—I do not wish to mention his name—would invariably be among those who blessed the couple. Though he called himself a man of progressive ideas, in the name of humour he would mock educated women merely to make the wedding guests laugh.

segments.text: He would say that when educated women entered the kitchen, they would first wash the brinjals with soap so that the brinjal fry would be clean. He would say that, because germs might cling to the knives used to cut vegetables, they would wash those knives with
“Dettol.”
The poet had repeated this very joke three times at weddings held in that house.

segments.text: See how undesirable it becomes to repeat what one has already said—to repeat it in the same town—and worse, at a wedding in the same house, or at a function!

segments.text: Some others too embrace failure by repeating what certain speakers have said, hoping to win the same praise from the people by speaking like them!

segments.text: When attacking the Congress rulers at meetings, I used to describe with a great flood of sorrow the incident in which a man named Punniyakodi, driven by poverty, fell into a well with his family and committed suicide. The people listening before me would shed tears!

blocks.text: When attacking the Congress rulers at meetings, I used to describe with a great flood of sorrow the incident in which a man named Punniyakodi, driven by poverty, fell into a well with his family and committed suicide. The people listening before me would shed tears!

segments.text: Not Punniyakodi and his wife alone: beginning with their eldest daughter, thirteen-year-old Manimekalai, down to a tender one-year-old child, all six children and their parents—eight people in all—became victims of poverty under this rule, I would say, speaking with emotion overflowing. My friend Dr. Ramayya, who attended meetings with me, was eager to speak on stages—and a good friend too!

segments.text: In the 1962 Legislative Assembly election he contested as a Kazhagam-backed candidate. At an election campaign meeting in his constituency, he decided to tell the Punniyakodi story and move the people to tears.

But the moment my doctor friend saw the crowd, he wanted to speak at length and launched into the Punniyakodi story.

segments.text: Speakers must develop a style of their own. Once people begin comparing them—
“he speaks like that man; he speaks like this man”
—they will stop listening to the speech itself and start watching the style being imitated.

segments.text: “ஒரு கணவனும் மனைவியும் ஒற்றுமையுடன் வாழ்ந்தார்கள். ஏழ்மை அவர்களைத் தாக்கியது. பிழைப்புக்கு வழியின்றித் தவித்தனர். ஒருநாள் மனைவி, தன் கணவனைப் பார்த்து வீட்டில் உள்ள காளை மாட்டைக் கொண்டு போய்ச் சந்தையில் விற்று அதில் கிடைக்கும் பணத்தைக் கொண்டு ஒரு பெட்டிக்கடை வைத்தால் குடும்பத்தை நகர்த்தலாமே என்று யோசனை கூறினாள். அவனும் உடன்பட்டு மாட்டை ஓட்டிக்கொண்டு சந்தைக்குச் செல்லும் சாலையில் நடந்தான். வழியில் மாடு அங்கு மிங்கும் மிரண்டு ஓடியது.

blocks.text: “A husband and wife lived in harmony. Poverty struck them. They suffered with no means of livelihood. One day the wife suggested to her husband that he take the bull at home to the market and sell it, and that with the money they could open a small petty shop and keep the family going. He agreed, drove the bull along, and walked down the road to the market. On the way, the bull became frightened and ran this way and that.

segments.text: Then a man driving a goat came along and said to him, ‘Ayya, why struggle with that unruly bull! Give it to me. I will give you my goat in return.’ The foolish husband gave away the bull, took the goat, and continued toward the market.

segments.text: A man came toward him holding a hen. He tricked the husband, saying that a hen could simply be carried in one's hand. The foolish husband agreed to that too, handed over the goat, took the hen, and set off toward the market.

segments.text: On the way—a biryani shop! The shopkeeper planned to buy the hen and cook it that very day. Speaking sweetly to the foolish husband, he bought the hen from him for a tumbler of tea.

segments.text: While the foolish husband was drinking the tea, his neighbour saw him and said, ‘You fool! I have been watching you all along. Having made this wager, the two returned home.

segments.text: The actor playing the head of the mutt at whom the ally of the poor said,
“You lie there eating—puffed up—bloated!”
had a body like a cluster bean. He appeared stooped and shrunken, all skin and bone. But the man who thundered,
“We have laboured and laboured until we are worn to the bone,”
looked hefty, with a paunch and belly, and appeared to weigh about three hundred pounds. Either the lines should have been changed, or at least the actors should have been changed to suit the roles.

segments.text: Perunthalaivar Kamarajar did not have the habit of arranging words into elegant Tamil sentence structures. But the way he approached the people's problems through his speech was distinctive. People listened eagerly to his long speeches because he was a leader speaking for them. His age, capacity for action, sacrifice, labour and influence—all these laid the foundation for his speech. Therefore, the people did not consider even the great simplicity of his speech a fault; they accepted what he said with satisfaction. If any speaker complains,
“I spoke like Perunthalaivar Kamarajar; why didn't the people listen eagerly?”
our answer is simply this: that speaker has not grown into Kamarajar!

blocks.text: In the early days when Arignar Anna first became known in Tamil Nadu as a speaker, alliterative word-chains would fall abundantly in his speech. But not one of those words was used without meaning merely to match “A” with “A” and “K” with “K”! When Anna said, “Periyar brought the Justice Party from the mansion to the maidan,” with that alliterative phrase he conveyed the historical truth that the party had been transformed into a party of the poor and the simple. He won the people's hearts.

segments.text: If the government imposed Section 144, he would not merely state the information and attack it. On the stage he would shower a question-arrow:
“In civilised countries, a law to cut out tongues?”

Seeing this, some thought it was enough for them too to become speakers by stringing together alliterative words. Whether it is alliterative phrasing or beautiful Tamil, while speaking it must pour out naturally; if one searches for such words and forces them into speech, one will meet only failure in the art of speaking.

என்ற நெல்லைத் தமிழும்,
“அந்தாண்டே! இந்தாண்டே”
என்ற தஞ்சைத் தமிழும்
“கீரியா? என்னப்பா பேப்பர் கீதா?”

segments.text: Twenty years ago, at a public meeting in Purasawalkam, Chennai, Professor Anbazhagan and I took part. When the Professor rose to speak, a woman handed him an infant and asked him to name the child. It was a girl! The Professor named her
“Karunanidhi.”

blocks.text: Twenty years ago, at a public meeting in Purasawalkam, Chennai, Professor Anbazhagan and I took part. When the Professor rose to speak, a woman handed him an infant and asked him to name the child. It was a girl! The Professor named her “Karunanidhi.” Karunanidhi is a name suited to people of every religion and to both men and women!

segments.text: At one time, even the wife of Mr. Bhaskaran, who helped develop the Dravidar movement in the Jayankonda Cholapuram area, was named Karunanidhi!
“Karunai—nidhi”
—that is, a treasury of grace, or a wealth of grace—is a name suited to any religion, to man or woman alike, isn't it? So when the Professor smiled and named that girl
“Karunanidhi,”
the whole meeting erupted in laughter!

segments.text: Then he finished speaking. I rose to speak. A mother came to me too with her baby girl and asked me to name her. I named that child
“Anbazhagi”
—and cooled the affectionate irritation I had felt toward the Professor.

segments.text: A speaker must be extremely careful even when naming children at meetings.

blocks.text: A speaker must be extremely careful even when naming children at meetings.

segments.text: Someone will bring a child! He will say,
“Give the child a name!”
To announce over the loudspeaker whose child is being given such-and-such a name, we look at him and ask what the child's father's name is. At once he says,
“I am!”
In the commotion he struggles to say his name. At last, somehow, he manages to give his name. It may be Abdul Rahman.

segments.text: One must find out what name he wants for the child—whether he wants a name suited specifically to Islam. If so, give a boy one of such names as Shah Jahan, Jahangir or Iqbal, and a girl one of such names as Nur Jahan, Mumtaz or Khadija. Hearing those names, the parents and their relatives will be happy!

“Rajarajan”

blocks.text: The Fifth World Tamil Conference was conducted in Madurai by the A.D.M.K. government. A Tourism Board hotel opened in connection with that conference was named “Rajarajan,” and large-scale publicity for it was carried out. A nameboard reading “Rajarajan” had already been placed on the front of the hotel. But suddenly, on the day of the opening, Chief Minister M.G.R. ordered that the name be removed.

segments.text: That act sent a great shock through the hearts of the people of Tamil Nadu.

blocks.text: That act sent a great shock through the hearts of the people of Tamil Nadu.

segments.text: At that time my tour programmes had been arranged in the Thanjai, Trichy and Pudukkottai districts. During those programmes, I named many of the baby boys brought to me on stages for naming
“Rajarajan.”
Immediately the crowds shouted,
“Long live Rajarajan!”

If even in naming a child one must learn to understand the feelings of the people and echo the sound of their hearts, is it not indispensable to develop the art of speaking so as to draw the people's attention to the many problems in the country?

segments.text: The Chennai Tamil of
“Eesthukinu po!”
, the Nellai Tamil of
“Ele! Vaale!”
, the Thanjai Tamil of
“Andhaande! Indhaande!”
, the North Arcot Tamil of
“Keeriya? Ennappa paper geetha?”

—Tamil changes in this way from district to district. But when those who speak such Tamil climb onto a stage, if they are good speakers, whatever district they belong to they will speak grammatical Tamil suited to the stage!

blocks.text: The Chennai Tamil of “Eesthukinu po!”, the Nellai Tamil of “Ele! Vaale!”, the Thanjai Tamil of “Andhaande! Indhaande!”, the North Arcot Tamil of “Keeriya? Ennappa paper geetha?”—Tamil changes in this way from district to district. But when those who speak such Tamil climb onto a stage, if they are good speakers, whatever district they belong to they will speak grammatical Tamil suited to the stage!

segments.text: Such is the power of the speaking platform! If any speaker disregards that power and uses on stage only the colloquial expressions he habitually uses, he will not find a place in the list of good speakers. His speech will be accepted only to the extent that he has conveyed the idea that had to be conveyed at that meeting. But he will not be accepted as a speaker.

A speaker from Thanjai district spoke there. He is not in the Kazhagam now. I hear he is in another party.

segments.text: To illustrate the poverty prevailing in the country, he used to collect and recount many incidents. At many meetings he had spoken, in exactly the sentence structure I have written here, of

“Eight comrades from Dindigul died after eating respected kathaalai tubers.”
The word

had jumped from the comrades to the kathaalai tubers! That is what comes of speaking in haste!

blocks.text: The great English scholar Addison was a celebrated figure in the eighteenth century. It is said that once, when he tried to speak, he stood there choking out “I conceive, conceive, conceive” three times! “Conceive” can mean “I think.” It can also mean “I am pregnant”!

segments.text: While Addison was struggling like this, someone in front is said to have risen and joked,
“Addison conceived three times! But he never gave birth to the child.”

segments.text: Speeches may be divided into a few such kinds. Historical speeches, scientific speeches, literary speeches, economic speeches—specialised speeches of these kinds generally find their proper place in seminars. For that, one must possess deep book-learning and experience in each subject. Otherwise, Valluvar's warning that it becomes like playing dice without a board becomes apt. The Tirukkural states categorically that one should not enter an assembly without fullness of learning.

segments.text: Some speakers wish to say at a meeting everything they know. If what they know is unknown to the people, there is nothing wrong in speaking about it! But there is a very great difference between what people do not know and what they cannot understand however much one speaks!

segments.text: தனக்கு என்ன விஷயங்கள் எல்லாம் தெரியும் என்பதை மேடையில் வீற்றிருக்கும் மற்ற பேச்சாளர்களுக்கு அல்லது தலைவர்களுக்கு உணர்த்துகிற பேச்சாக மட்டும் அமையாமல், எதிரே வீற்றிருக்கும் நூற்றுக்கணக்கான அல்லது ஆயிரக்கணக்கான மக்களுக்குப் பயன்படுகிற பேச்சாக அமைய வேண்டுமென்பதில் ஒரு பேச்சாளருக்கு மிகுந்த கவனம் தேவை. தனக்கும் அல்லது தன்னைப்போல் நிறைய நூல்களைப் படித்தவர்களுக்கும் மட்டுமே தெரிந்திருக்கக்கூடிய செய்திகளையோ, குறிப்புகளையோ—மக்களுக்கும் தெரியவைக்க வேண்டுமென்றால் அதற்கேற்றவாறு இடமும்—இடத்திற்கு ஏற்றவாறு எடுத்துக் கொண்ட பொருளும் இருந்திட வேண்டும்.

segments.text: மாநில சுயாட்சிக் கோரிக்கையை வலியுறுத்திப் பேச வேண்டிய கூட்டம் என்று வைத்துக்கொள்வோம். அரசியல் சட்டப்படி, எத்தனை அதிகாரங்கள் மத்திய அரசுப் பட்டியலில், எத்தனை அதிகாரங்கள் மாநில அரசுப் பட்டியலில், எத்தனை அதிகாரங்கள் பொதுப் பட்டியலில்—என்ற விபரங்களையும்; அரசியல் சட்டத்தின் எந்தப் பிரிவின்படி மத்திய அரசு, ஒரு மாநில ஆட்சியைக் கவிழ்க்க முடியும் என்பதையும் — அரசியல் சட்டம் தொகுத்த அறிஞர்களில் ஒருவரான அம்பேத்கார் அவர்களே அந்தச் சட்டம் தலைகீழ் மாற்றத்திற்கு உட்படுத்தப்பட வேண்டுமெனக் கருத்தறிவித்ததையும் — மாநில சுயாட்சி பற்றி இராசமன்னார் குழுவினர் ஆராய்ந்து அளித்த அறிக்கையினையும்—அதைத் தி.மு.க. ஆட்சிக் காலத்தில் பரிசீலித்து சட்டமன்றத்திலேயே மாநில சுயாட்சித் தீர்மானம் நிறைவேற்றியதையும்—மாநிலங்கள் சுயாட்சித் தன்மையுடன் திகழவேண்டுமென்று பண்டித நேரு அவர்கள் வலியுறுத்திக் குறிப்பிட்டதையும்—ஆதாரங்களுடன்—தேதிகளுடன் எடுத்துச் சொல்ல விரும்புகிற ஒரு பேச்சாளர்; அவர் சென்னையிலே ஒரு மேடையிலே நின்று பேசுகிறார் என்றாலுங்கூட — சென்னையில் எந்தப் பகுதி என்பதை நினைவில் வைத்துக் கொண்டு பேசவேண்டும்.

segments.text: ஒருவர், ஒரு முக்கியமான பொறுப்பில் அமர்ந்திருப்பவர், முக்கியமானவர்கள் நிரம்பிய ஒரு அவையில் பேசினார். தமிழகத்தில் வெள்ளம் புயல் ஏற்பட்டு பல பகுதிகள் சேதமுற்றது பற்றி விவாதம் நடந்தது. அந்த முக்கியமானவர் பேசும்போது சொன்னார்,
“என்னுடைய சிறு வயதில் சென்னையில் பெரு வெள்ளத்தை நேரில் பார்த்தேன்”
என்று. அத்துடன் நிறுத்தவில்லை.
“எனக்கு எழுபது வயதிருக்கும். அப்போதுதான் சென்னையில் எம்டன் குண்டு விழுந்த நேரம். பெரிய மழை பெய்து ஏரிகள் எல்லாம் உடைத்துக் கொண்டு சென்னை நகரமே மூழ்கிவிடும் போலிருந்தது”
என்று விவரித்தார். ஒரு பெரியவர் குறுக்கிட்டு,
“எம்டன் குண்டு விழுந்தது 1914-ஆம் ஆண்டில் அல்லவா?”
என்றார்!
“உங்களுக்குத் தெரியாது. எனக்கு நன்றாக நினைவிருக்கிறது. நான் ஏழு வயதுச் சிறுவன்”
என்றார் திட்டவட்டமாக அந்த முக்கியமானவர்!

segments.text: A speaker must take great care that his speech does not merely show the other speakers or leaders on the stage how much he knows; it must be useful to the hundreds or thousands of people seated before him. segments.text: Suppose it is a meeting at which one must speak in support of the demand for State autonomy. A speaker may wish to explain, with evidence and dates, how many powers under the Constitution are in the Union List, how many in the State List, how many in the Concurrent List; under which provision the Union government can bring down a State government; how Ambedkar himself, one of the scholars who framed the Constitution, expressed the view that the Constitution should be turned upside down and changed; the report submitted by the Rajamannar Committee after examining State autonomy; how, during D.M.K. rule, that report was considered and a State-autonomy resolution passed in the Legislative Assembly itself; and how Pandit Nehru stressed that the States should possess an autonomous character. Even if such a speaker is standing on a platform in Chennai, he must remember which part of Chennai he is speaking in.

segments.text: A person occupying an important position once spoke in an assembly filled with important people. There was a discussion about floods and storms in Tamil Nadu that had damaged many areas. While speaking, that important person said,
“When I was young, I saw a great flood in Chennai with my own eyes.”
He did not stop there.
“I must have been seventy years old. That was when the Emden bomb fell in Chennai. Heavy rain poured down; all the lakes breached, and it seemed the whole city of Chennai would be submerged,”
he explained. An elder interrupted:
“Did not the Emden bomb fall in 1914?”
“You do not know. I remember it very well. I was a seven-year-old boy,”
the important person declared firmly!

segments.text: “Two days ago I received a telephone message from a police station. They said a man had been arrested because he had drunk, and that someone had come to bail him out. I ordered that if anyone came to bail out the drunkard, he too should be arrested. That is this Ramachandran.”

segments.text: ஒருமணி நேரப் பேச்சில் அப்படிக் கடுஞ்சொல் கூறிக் கண்டிப்பது ஓரிரு வினாடிகளே இருக்கவேண்டுமே தவிர, முழுப் பேச்சும் கடுஞ்சொற்களின் கோர்வை ஆகிவிடுமேயானால் ஒருக்கணம் மின்வெட்டுப்போலப் பளிச்சிட்டுத் தெரிந்த அந்தக் கடுஞ்சொல்லுக்குரிய மதிப்பு இல்லாமல் போய்விடக் கூடும்.

segments.text: அரசியல் மேடைகளில் கடுஞ்சொற்கள் இருதரப்பிலிருந்தும் கணைகளாகக் கிளம்பலாம். அதற்காகப் பேச்சு முழுமையுமே கடுஞ்சொற் களஞ்சியமாகவும்—ஆபாசக் குட்டையாகவும் அமைந்திடுமேயானால்; விரைவில் அந்தப் பேச்சாளர்களும் இருக்குமிடந் தெரியாமல் போய்விடுவர்; அவர்கள் சார்ந்துள்ள கட்சிகளும் சிறப்பு குன்றிச் செயலிழந்து நின்றுவிடும்.

segments.text: மேடையில் மக்களின் பிரச்சினைகளை ஒன்றோடொன்று தொடர்புபடுத்தி எடுத்து வைக்க வேண்டும். அவ்வப்போது எழுகின்ற விவாதத்திற்குரிய விஷயங்களை அவரவர் கட்சிக் கண்ணோட்டத்திற்கேற்ப மக்களிடம் விளக்கிட வேண்டும். பல்வேறு அரசியல் கட்சிக் கொள்கைகளுக்கும் தனது கட்சிக் கொள்கைகளுக்குமுள்ள வேறுபாடுகள் பற்றியும், உடன்பாடுகள் பற்றியும் வாதங்களை அடுக்கிடவேண்டும். நாட்டில் பற்றி எரிகிற ஒரு முக்கியமான பிரச்சினையைத் தனது கட்சி எவ்வாறு அணுகுகிறது என்பதைத் தெளிவாக மக்களிடம் கூறவேண்டும்.

segments.text: இவ்வளவையும் விட்டுவிட்டு, மேடையில் ஏறியதும் தனது கட்சித் தலைவனுக்கு ஒரு பகுதி நேரம் பாராட்டு—மறு பகுதி நேரம் மாற்றுக் கட்சித் தலைவர்களுக்கு ஆபாச அர்ச்சனை—என்ற நிலையில் பேச்சாளர், தனது சொற்பொழிவை அமைத்துக்கொண்டால்; கூட்டத்தில் மேடைக்கருகே இருக்கிற தனது கட்சிக்காரர்களின் கைத்தட்டலை மட்டுமே பெறமுடியும். பொதுவான மக்களின் பாராட்டு அந்தப் பேச்சுக்குக் கிடைக்காது.

segments.text: “வசவு”

ஒன்றையே தனது பேச்சுப் பாணியாக ஆக்கிக் கொண்டவர்களில் பல பேர், அடிக்கடி அரசியல் கட்சிகள் பலவற்றுக்குத் தாவுகிறவர்களாகவும் இருந்திடக் காண்கிறோம். கொள்கை, இலட்சியம், எந்த அடிப்படையும் இல்லாத சந்தர்ப்பவாதிகள் அவர்கள்! பேச்சால் மட்டுமே பிழைப்பு நடத்துகிறவர்கள். அவர்கள் கட்சி மேடையானாலும்—அல்லது யார் வீட்டுத் திருமண மேடையானாலும்—அல்லது எந்தப் பொது நிகழ்ச்சியானாலும்—சுற்றுச் சூழல் பற்றிக் கவலை கொள்ளாமல்; தரக்குறைவான, ஆபாசமான, மிகத் தீவிரவாதிகளைப் போலக் கடுமையான வார்த்தைகளை வாரியிறைப்பர்.

segments.text: சில நாட்கள் கழித்துப் பார்த்தால், அதே பேச்சாளர் வேறு மேடையில்—வேறு கட்சியில்! அதன்பிறகு சில வாரங்கள் சென்று பார்த்தால், அதே பேச்சாளர், இன்னொரு கட்சியில்—இன்னொரு மேடையில்! இப்படியே அவர்கள் பல கட்சிகளுக்குப் பாய்ந்து மக்களின் மதிப்பீட்டில் மிகக்கேவலமாகத் தேய்ந்து போய்விடுகிறார்கள்.

segments.text: நான் பதினைந்து வயதுச் சிறுவனாக இருந்தபோது நடந்த ஒரு நிகழ்ச்சி! திருவாரூரில் ஒரு பொதுக்கூட்டத்தில் உருக்கமும் உணர்ச்சியும் பொங்கிட ஒரு பெரியவர் முழங்கினார். மக்கள் எழுச்சியுடன் அவர் பேச்சைக் கேட்டனர். மறுநாள் அதிகாலையில் நான் நண்பர்களுடன் திருவாரூர் ஓடம் போக்கி ஆற்றுமணலில் நடந்து சென்று கொண்டிருந்தேன். எதிரே மணலில் ஒரு மனித உருவம் ஆடை குலைந்த நிலையில் படுத்திருந்தது. அருகே சென்று பார்த்தோம். முதல் நாளிரவு மேடையில் முழங்கிய அதே மனிதர்தான். நன்றாகக் குடித்துவிட்டு ஆற்று மணலில் உருண்டு கிடக்கிறார். அந்தக் காட்சியை பார்க்கிறவர்கள் அவரை மட்டுமல்ல; அவர் எந்தக் கட்சிக்காகப் பேச வந்தாரோ—அந்தக் கட்சியையும் கடுகளவாவது மதிப்பார்களா?

segments.text: Political speakers have multiplied. But among them, the number who understand literature gives little cause for cheer. Have they at least studied history deeply? Even that number is small! Many speakers train themselves only to abuse members of rival parties crudely, and then climb onto the stage.

segments.text: Speaking harshly—with biting force—is one thing!

segments.text: Speaking crudely—obscenely—in a disgusting manner is another!

segments.text: An unavoidable situation may arise in which a speaker has to use harsh words. Someone speaking on a rival party's platform may spread a slander, refuse to take responsibility for proving it, and make it his occupation deliberately to fling dust and abuse at others. When a speaker affected by that, or the political party to which he belongs, replies from the stage, strong condemnation may become unavoidable.

segments.text: In a one-hour speech, such a harsh word of condemnation should last only a second or two. If the whole speech becomes a chain of harsh words, the harsh expression that flashed for an instant like a streak of lightning may itself lose its value.

segments.text: On political platforms, harsh words may fly like arrows from both sides. But if the whole speech becomes a treasury of harsh words—and a pool of obscenity—the speakers will soon disappear without anyone knowing where they are, and the parties they belong to will lose distinction and stand ineffective.

segments.text: On the stage, the people's problems must be presented in relation to one another. Issues that arise for debate from time to time must be explained to the people according to each party's viewpoint. Arguments must be set out about the differences and agreements between the policies of various political parties and one's own party. One must clearly tell the people how one's party approaches a major issue burning in the country.

segments.text: If, abandoning all this, a speaker climbs onto the stage and spends one part of his time praising his own party leader and another part performing an obscene ritual of abuse against rival party leaders, he can win only the applause of his own party people standing near the stage. Such a speech will not win the praise of the general public.

segments.text: An incident from when I was a fifteen-year-old boy! At a public meeting in Thiruvarur, an elder thundered with pathos and emotion overflowing. The people listened to his speech with rising enthusiasm. Early the next morning, I was walking with friends along the sands of the Odam Pokki river at Thiruvarur. Ahead of us lay a human figure on the sand, clothes dishevelled. We went closer and looked. It was the very same man who had thundered from the stage the previous night. He had drunk heavily and lay rolling on the river sand. Would those who saw that sight respect, even by a mustard-seed's measure, not only him but also the party for which he had come to speak?

என்று கேட்டுக்கொண்டே மேடையிலிருந்து இறங்குவோம் என்று அவர்களே பலமுறை சொல்லக் கேட்டிருக்கிறேன். இல்லாவிட்டால் திரும்பி ஊருக்குச் செல்ல வழிச்செலவுப் பணத்திற்கு என்ன செய்வது? யாரைத் தேடுவது? அதனால்தான் செயலாளர் கைகளை அன்போடும் பாசத்தோடும் கெட்டியாகப் பிடித்துக்கொண்டு பேச்சை முடிப்பார்களாம்!

segments.text: At a night public meeting, the speaker thunders before thousands. In the morning, he is escorted to the railway station or bus stand to be sent off. A cigarette between his fingers! A cloud of smoke pouring through mouth and nose! If some of those who watched, enjoyed and praised him at the previous night's public meeting happen to see him there, their respect and regard for him are bound to fall a little.

segments.text: I believe these one or two examples are enough. Speakers of a movement very much need the resolve and determination that, for the movement they have embraced—for the policy they have accepted—they must sacrifice certain habits.

blocks.text: I believe these one or two examples are enough. Speakers of a movement very much need the resolve and determination that, for the movement they have embraced—for the policy they have accepted—they must sacrifice certain habits.

segments.text: In any party or large organisation, speakers have a special place. A circle of cadres surrounds them. Speakers must have the awareness that it is on the stage arranged by those cadres that we shine as speakers.

blocks.text: In any party or large organisation, speakers have a special place. A circle of cadres surrounds them. Speakers must have the awareness that it is on the stage arranged by those cadres that we shine as speakers.

segments.text: Speakers must not think of themselves as the masters of a movement or large organisation and treat cadres like servants. A feeling of comradeship must grow and overflow.

blocks.text: Speakers must not think of themselves as the masters of a movement or large organisation and treat cadres like servants. A feeling of comradeship must grow and overflow.

segments.text: The cadre shakes a collection box, gathers one paisa and two paisa at a time, sends money for the speaker's travel expenses, prints publicity posters, stays awake night and day, applies paste with his own hands and sticks them up, climbs poles and trees without regard for danger to tie festoons, puts up the stage, arranges the loudspeaker—and finally, if he hears that the speaker is not coming, how deeply he will be disheartened is something only those who have laboured, and those who still labour, as cadres to build a movement can understand. Speakers must not give such disappointments to their party cadres. Except for unavoidable, unforeseen and genuine reasons, agreed engagements should not be cancelled.

segments.text: Speakers and meeting organisers must rid themselves of these shortcomings that have crept into every party.

segments.text: Annan C. P. Chitrarasu, who served as Chairman of the Legislative Council, and Annan Alagirisami—the whirlwind of the Self-Respect Movement, the commander of the Self-Respect cause—when bringing their speeches to a close at meetings, would tightly hold the hand of the party secretary on the stage, look at the people, and say,
“Think deeply about all that has been said so far and come to a conclusion!”

I have heard them themselves tell this story many times. Otherwise, what were they to do for travel money to get back home? Whom were they to look for? That was why, it seems, they ended the speech holding the secretary's hand tightly—with love and affection!

segments.text: Valluvar states categorically that we must know that no other word can defeat our word—and, after examining and knowing this, expand our idea only with the word we have carefully chosen.

segments.text: From the moment a speaker stands before the microphone until he finishes his speech, he is duty-bound to preserve and uphold the dignity of that stage and the respect due to the art of speaking.

segments.text: While one is speaking, some boy or girl in the crowd may get up and try to leave. The speaker should simply go on as though he has not noticed it. If, in anger, he blurts out something like,
“Hey! Who's that? Sit down! Hey, you there! Drive those saniyans away!”
the standard of that speaker will fall very low.

segments.text: In the early days when I began speaking on stages, I took part in many meetings in Adi Dravidar colonies. Once, at ten at night, a friend named Shamsudeen and I went to speak at a colony. About two hundred people had gathered. Shamsudeen was older than I was! He also had more political experience than I did! That meeting was at the Adi Dravidar colony near the Naalukaal Mandapam in Thiruvarur. Shamsudeen began to speak. An elderly man in the crowd was sitting there with great interest, enjoying the speeches.

blocks.text: In the early days when I began speaking on stages, I took part in many meetings in Adi Dravidar colonies. Once, at ten at night, a friend named Shamsudeen and I went to speak at a colony. About two hundred people had gathered. Shamsudeen was older than I was! He also had more political experience than I did! That meeting was at the Adi Dravidar colony near the Naalukaal Mandapam in Thiruvarur. Shamsudeen began to speak. An elderly man in the crowd was sitting there with great interest, enjoying the speeches.

segments.text: But the poor man had a cough! He kept coughing often. Shamsudeen could not tolerate the interruption to his speech caused by the man's coughing. Two or three times he looked at the old man and snapped,
“Shoo! Keep quiet!”
Poor man—he could neither stop coughing nor did he leave the meeting.

segments.text: The old man coughed once more. That was enough: Shamsudeen suddenly picked up the small vessel of tea on the table and poured it over the old man's head.

segments.text: That incident caused a great commotion in the meeting, and I and the other friends had to calm everyone down.

segments.text: Whatever the interruptions, speakers must ignore them and keep their attention on the ideas they have to present. At the same time, organisers of meetings must also take advance care to maintain order on and around the stage through cadres.

segments.text: When speakers whom the people eagerly await are seated on the stage, if some speakers go on extending their own speeches right in front of them, keeping the awaited speakers sitting there, the people will lose patience.

segments.text: The late Agriculture Minister A. Govindasamy, before he assumed ministerial office, arranged a meeting at Devapandalam in Thennaarkadu district and took me there. Another speaker had also been invited with us. That speaker had long been associated with the movement. He was someone we held in a position of respect. But he did not possess the ability to draw people through his speech!

blocks.text: The late Agriculture Minister A. Govindasamy, before he assumed ministerial office, arranged a meeting at Devapandalam in Thennaarkadu district and took me there. Another speaker had also been invited with us. That speaker had long been associated with the movement. He was someone we held in a position of respect. But he did not possess the ability to draw people through his speech!

segments.text: A huge crowd had gathered like a flood. The whole town wore a festive look. Thiru. Govindasamy spoke briefly and pleasantly and finished. Next, the speaker I mentioned earlier rose. He spoke—and spoke—and kept on speaking.

blocks.text: A huge crowd had gathered like a flood. The whole town wore a festive look. Thiru. Govindasamy spoke briefly and pleasantly and finished. Next, the speaker I mentioned earlier rose. He spoke—and spoke—and kept on speaking.

segments.text: The crowd lost patience. Perhaps the people began to doubt whether he would give me a chance to speak at all!

blocks.text: The crowd lost patience. Perhaps the people began to doubt whether he would give me a chance to speak at all!

segments.text: From the middle of the crowd, a man wearing a turban stood up. With folded hands, he called loudly toward the stage:

segments.text: “Ayya! Periyavangale! We have come from eighteen miles away to hear his speech. Could you please sit down for a little while?”

blocks.text: “Ayya! Periyavangale! We have come from eighteen miles away to hear his speech. Could you please sit down for a little while?”

segments.text: I was shocked to hear that. The crowd welcomed the turbaned man's request with applause. The speaker became angry.

blocks.text: I was shocked to hear that. The crowd welcomed the turbaned man's request with applause. The speaker became angry.

segments.text: “Oh, is that so, appa! Here, I am sitting down!”

blocks.text: “Oh, is that so, appa! Here, I am sitting down!”

segments.text: He dropped abruptly into a chair. He did not stop there. Turning to me, he insisted,
“Karunanidhi! You must not speak at this meeting! Finish in just one line! Only then will these fellows learn some sense.”

blocks.text: He dropped abruptly into a chair. He did not stop there. Turning to me, he insisted, “Karunanidhi! You must not speak at this meeting! Finish in just one line! Only then will these fellows learn some sense.”

segments.text: I rose to speak. For about fifteen minutes of my opening remarks, I spoke only about his greatness. Whose greatness? The greatness of the very speaker whom that turbaned man had made sit down! I spoke with feeling, saying that it was because of the work done by people like him that all of us had become known to the people today. Only after I saw lines of happiness shine on his face did I leave that subject and begin speaking about politics. I finished after speaking for about an hour and a half.

“Your speech today was wonderful.”

segments.text: அறிஞர் அண்ணா அவர்கள் பேசும்போது, வலப்புறமும் இடப்புறமுமாக உடலைத் திருப்புவார். கைகள் லேசாக உயரும், தாழும்! பொடிபோடும் வழக்கம் அவருக்கு உண்டு. சட்டையின் பக்கவாட்டுப் பையில் ஒருகை நுழைந்திருக்கும். அவரது பேச்சின் சுவையில் திளைத்த மக்கள் கையொலி செய்து ஆரவாரம் புரியும்போது, சட்டைப் பையிலுள்ள பொடி டப்பாவிலிருக்கும் பொடியை யாருக்கும் தெரியாமல் மூக்கில் திணித்துக்கொண்டு மேல்துண்டினால் ஏதோ வியர்வை துடைப்பது போலத் துடைத்துக் கொண்டே தொடர்ந்து பேசிக்கொண்டேயிருப்பார்.

segments.text: The distinctive manner or individual style called
“mannerism”

can take hold of speakers as well. As they speak, distinctive bodily gestures and unavoidable habits begin without their even realising it; later, those very things become characteristics peculiar to those speakers.

segments.text: Some stand on the stage without dancing or moving, pouring out ideas like a waterfall.

segments.text: When Arignar Anna spoke, he would turn his body to the right and left. His hands would rise and fall slightly! He had the habit of taking snuff. One hand would be inside the side pocket of his shirt. When the people, immersed in the flavour of his speech, applauded and cheered, he would, without anyone noticing, take snuff from the box in his shirt pocket and push it into his nose, then wipe with his upper cloth as though he were wiping sweat, and continue speaking.

segments.text: Thanthai Periyar, in his later years, spoke only while seated! I was one of those who had gone to meetings with him during the period when he spoke standing. segments.text: இப்போது வயது நாற்பத்தி ஆறு: தோற்றம் வயதைத் தெரிவிக்காது என்றாலும் நன்கு முதிர்ச்சி பெற்ற கருத்துக்களை மேடைகளில் வாரி வழங்கிக் கொண்டிருக்கிறார். சற்றுக் குனிந்து வளைந்த, ஆனால் யாருக்கும் வளையாத கொள்கைகளை அள்ளித் தருகிறார். கறுப்புச் சட்டை மேனியை அலங்கரிக்கிறது. கையில் சொற்பொழிவுக்கான குறிப்புகள். அருகேயுள்ள மேஜையிலே அன்றைய பேச்சுக்கான ஆதாரங்களை எடுத்துக் கூறுவதற்கு வாய்ப்பான பெரிய பெரிய புத்தகங்கள்.
“இங்கேதான் நீங்கள் முக்கியமாகக் கவனிக்க வேண்டும். அதுதான் முக்கியமானது; மிக முக்கியமானது”
என்ற சொற்றொடர் அடிக்கடி பேச்சினிடையே வந்து கொண்டிருக்கிறது. மணிக்கணக்கில் பேசுகிறார். யார் இவர்?

blocks.text: இப்போது வயது நாற்பத்தி ஆறு: தோற்றம் வயதைத் தெரிவிக்காது என்றாலும் நன்கு முதிர்ச்சி பெற்ற கருத்துக்களை மேடைகளில் வாரி வழங்கிக் கொண்டிருக்கிறார். சற்றுக் குனிந்து வளைந்த, ஆனால் யாருக்கும் வளையாத கொள்கைகளை அள்ளித் தருகிறார். கறுப்புச் சட்டை மேனியை அலங்கரிக்கிறது. கையில் சொற்பொழிவுக்கான குறிப்புகள். அருகேயுள்ள மேஜையிலே அன்றைய பேச்சுக்கான ஆதாரங்களை எடுத்துக் கூறுவதற்கு வாய்ப்பான பெரிய பெரிய புத்தகங்கள். “இங்கேதான் நீங்கள் முக்கியமாகக் கவனிக்க வேண்டும். அதுதான் முக்கியமானது; மிக முக்கியமானது” என்ற சொற்றொடர் அடிக்கடி பேச்சினிடையே வந்து கொண்டிருக்கிறது. மணிக்கணக்கில் பேசுகிறார். யார் இவர்?

segments.text: வேறு யாருமல்ல: தனது பத்தாவது வயதிலேயே திராவிடர் இயக்க மேடைகளில் பேச ஆரம்பித்தவர்—இன்றைய திராவிடர் கழகப் பொதுச்செயலாளர்—விடுதலை நாளிதழின் ஆசிரியர்—வீரமணி அவர்களைத்தான் குறிப்பிடுகிறேன்.

segments.text: பத்து வயது முதற்கொண்டே பெரியாருடன் பணிபுரிந்து கொண்டு—பள்ளியிலும் பயின்று—கல்லூரியிலும் பட்டம் பெற்று—திராவிடர் கழகத்தின் ஒப்பற்ற தொண்டராகவும் விளங்கிய வீரமணி, இளந்தளிர்ப் பருவத்திலே மேடையிலே பேசுகிற வியப்புமிகு நிகழ்ச்சியைக் காணப் பெருங்கூட்டம் திரளும்.

segments.text: பெரியாரின் தலைமையை ஏற்றுக் கொண்டோம் என்பது மட்டுமல்லாமல்—அவருடனேயே இருந்து—அவருடனேயே சுற்றுப்பயணம் நிகழ்ச்சிகளுக்குச் சென்று—அவரது குடிஅரசு, விடுதலை, பகுத்தறிவு ஏடுகளின் அலுவலகங்களில் பணிபுரிந்து—அவரது கொள்கைகளை எழுத்து வாயிலாகவும், பேச்சின் மூலமும் மக்களிடம் பரப்பிய பல தலைவர்கள் உண்டு.

segments.text: ஆனால், பல சிறுவர், சிறுமியர்—ஏதோ தாங்கள் பெற்றோர் ஆசைக்காக—உற்றார் உறவினர் விருப்பத்திற்காக—அல்லது அந்தச் சிறுவர்களே அதை ஒரு
“மேனரிசம்”

ஆக எடுத்துக்கொண்டு, மேடைகளில் யாரையோ தாக்கியோ, புகழ்ந்தோ பேசிவிட்டு கைத்தட்டலைப் பெற்று விட எண்ணுகிறார்களே தவிர, தங்களுடைய கல்விப் பயிற்சியை வளர்த்துக் கொள்ளவும், தெளிவாகத் தெரிந்து கொள்ளவும் முயற்சிப்பதில்லை.

segments.text: பெரியாரின் அண்ணன் மகனார் தோழர் ஈ.வெ.கி. சம்பத், இளம்வயதிலேயே அண்ணாவுடன் நெருங்கிப் பழகி—
“சொல்லின் செல்வர்”

என்ற சிறப்புப் பெறுகிற அளவுக்குப் பேச்சாளராக விளங்கினார். கொள்கையில் நிலைத்த நெஞ்சமில்லாத காரணத்தால் அவரது அரிய ஆற்றலைத் தமிழகம் முழுமையாகப் பயன்படுத்திக்கொள்ள முடியவில்லை. இயற்கை, அவரை முழுவாழ்வு வாழ விடாமல் நம்மிடமிருந்து பறித்துக்கொண்டு விட்டது. திராவிடர் இயக்கம், தமிழ் தேசியக் கட்சி, காங்கிரஸ் என்று கட்சி மாற்றங்கள் அவருக்கு ஏற்பட்டபோதிலும் வீருகொண்ட விரிவுரையாளராகத் திகழ்ந்தார்.

segments.text: அவரை எதிர்த்துத் தி.மு.கழகச் சார்பில் 1962-ல் தென்சென்னையில் போட்டியிட்டு வெற்றி பெற்ற நாஞ்சிலார் என்னும் நாஞ்சில் கி. மனோகரன் அவர்கள், அவருக்கு ஈடுகொடுக்கும் சொல் வல்லாராகத் திகழ்ந்தவர்—இப்போது மின்வெட்டுப் போன்ற மிடுக்கான பேச்சுக்கு எடுத்துக்காட்டாக இருக்கிற அவர், தனது இளம் பிராயத்திலேயே மேடைகளில் முழங்கிடத் தொடங்கியவர்தான்!

segments.text: மிக இளம் பருவம் எனக் கூறமுடியாவிட்டாலும்—கட்டிளம் காளையாக மேடையேறிக் கனல் தெறிக்கும் சொற்களால் மக்களைக் கவர்ந்து கடினமான விஷயங்களையும் பெரியார் பாணியில் மிக விரிவாக எடுத்துரைத்து
“வாலிபப் பெரியார்”
என்றே அழைக்கப்பட்ட வசீகரமிகு பேச்சழகர் எ.வி.பி. ஆசைத்தம்பி அவர்கள், மறைந்து விட்டார் எனினும் அவரது எழுத்து, பேச்சு ஆகிய தொண்டுகளை மறந்திட இயலுமோ!

segments.text: “பேசும் கலை வளர்ப்போம்”

என்ற இந்தக் கட்டுரைத் தொடர் வாயிலாக, எளிய நடையில் பல இனிய நிகழ்ச்சிகளையும்—இதயத்தைத் தொடும் நிகழ்ச்சிகளையும்—பல்வேறு துறைகளிலும் இயக்கத்திலும் உள்ள திறமை வாய்ந்த பேச்சாளர்களைப் பற்றியும்—எப்படிப் பேச வேண்டும், பேசக் கூடாது என்பன போன்ற கருத்துக்களையும்—என்னால் இயன்ற அளவு எடுத்துக் கூறியிருக்கின்றேன்.

segments.text: He is now forty-six years old. Though his appearance does not reveal his age, he is pouring out well-matured ideas on platforms. Slightly stooped and bent, he nevertheless offers principles that bend to no one. A black shirt adorns his body. In his hand are notes for the speech. On the nearby table lie large books useful for citing evidence for that day's speech.
“This is where you must pay particular attention. That is the important point; the very important point”
—this phrase keeps recurring in his speech. He speaks for hours. Who is he?

segments.text: None other than the man who began speaking on Dravidar movement platforms at the age of ten—the present General Secretary of the Dravidar Kazhagam—the editor of the daily Viduthalai—Veeramani.

blocks.text: None other than the man who began speaking on Dravidar movement platforms at the age of ten—the present General Secretary of the Dravidar Kazhagam—the editor of the daily Viduthalai—Veeramani.

segments.text: From the age of ten, Veeramani worked with Periyar while continuing his schooling, earned a college degree, and became an incomparable worker of the Dravidar Kazhagam. In his tender young years, great crowds would gather to witness the astonishing sight of him speaking on a stage.

segments.text: Many leaders did more than merely accept Periyar's leadership: they stayed with him, travelled with him to programmes, worked in the offices of his Kudi Arasu, Viduthalai and Pagutharivu journals, and carried his principles to the people through writing and speech.

blocks.text: Many leaders did more than merely accept Periyar's leadership: they stayed with him, travelled with him to programmes, worked in the offices of his Kudi Arasu, Viduthalai and Pagutharivu journals, and carried his principles to the people through writing and speech.

segments.text: As times changed, they may have gone to different movements. Yet they themselves neither forgot nor concealed that the training they received from Periyar was the reason they were—and are—respected as leaders, speakers and writers!

blocks.text: As times changed, they may have gone to different movements. Yet they themselves neither forgot nor concealed that the training they received from Periyar was the reason they were—and are—respected as leaders, speakers and writers!

segments.text: Likewise, there are those who not only accepted the leadership of Perarignar Anna, who had Periyar as his leader, but spoke with him, joined him on long tours, stayed close to him without parting, trained under him, and acquired many abilities!

blocks.text: Likewise, there are those who not only accepted the leadership of Perarignar Anna, who had Periyar as his leader, but spoke with him, joined him on long tours, stayed close to him without parting, trained under him, and acquired many abilities!

segments.text: There are also those who had the opportunity to train under both Periyar and Anna—and dedicated themselves to the ideals laid down by the two! They have every reason to be proud of that rare blessing! There are a few who, like me, can think with joy: I too had a place in that group!

segments.text: Today, seeing very young boys and girls speak on stages has become common at meetings of every party—why, even at religious meetings.

blocks.text: Today, seeing very young boys and girls speak on stages has become common at meetings of every party—why, even at religious meetings.

segments.text: But many boys and girls—whether to satisfy their parents, please relatives, or because they themselves have taken it up as a
“mannerism”
—think only of attacking someone or praising someone on stage and collecting applause. They make no effort to develop their education and to understand things clearly.

blocks.text: But many boys and girls—whether to satisfy their parents, please relatives, or because they themselves have taken it up as a “mannerism”—think only of attacking someone or praising someone on stage and collecting applause. They make no effort to develop their education and to understand things clearly.

segments.text: Such boys and girls should think about how our friend Veeramani, even at a young age, worked without pause, cared about his education, remained loyal to his leader, and likewise stood firm in principle.

segments.text: Comrade E. V. K. Sampath, Periyar's elder brother's son, became closely associated with Anna while still young and grew into such a speaker that he earned the distinction
“Sollin Selvar.”

Because he lacked a steadfast heart in policy, Tamil Nadu could not fully make use of his rare ability. Nature took him away from us before allowing him to live a full life. Though he underwent party changes—from the Dravidar movement to the Tamil National Party and then the Congress—he remained a spirited public speaker.

segments.text: Though one cannot call it extremely young, E. V. P. Aasai Thambi mounted the stage as a sturdy young bull, captivated people with spark-scattering words, explained difficult matters at great length in Periyar's style, and was called
“Vaaliba Periyar.”
Though that captivatingly eloquent speaker has passed away, can his service through writing and speech be forgotten!

segments.text: Through this series of articles,
“Let Us Develop the Art of Speaking,”

I have, to the extent I could, presented in a simple style many pleasant incidents—incidents that touch the heart—speakers of ability from many fields and movements—and thoughts on how one should speak and how one should not.

segments.text: If this series proves useful even to some extent to those who wish to excel in the art of speaking, I shall be greatly pleased.
